clue.text: Monster giving a headsman little satisfaction

definitions.text: Monster giving a headsman little satisfaction

parts.words: Monster giving a headsman little satisfaction
parts.note: the many-headed beast of Greek myth grew two new heads for every one cut off, so an executioner would get nowhere

explanation.surface: An executioner is left frustrated by some beast.
explanation.definitionFit: The serpent killed by Heracles grew back two heads for each one severed, so beheading it was futile.

clue.text: Its victim may hop in a frenzy

definitions.text: Its victim may hop in a frenzy

indicators.note: a frenzy throws things into wild disorder, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone suffering an affliction might jump about wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frenzy' rearranges MAYHOPINA; the whole clue also describes the condition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mild form of mania brings elation and overactivity, the kind of state that sets someone leaping about.

clue.text: Some cleaners are so off-putting to chaps

definitions.note: the clue's adjective stands for the verb meaning to put off

indicators.note: cleaners are so named because the word splits into a first part plus the word for chaps

parts.note: detergents are cleaning agents
gents are chaps

explanation.surface: Cleaning products are said to repel men.
explanation.walkthrough: Read DETERGENTS as DETER-GENTS: off-putting to chaps. Remove GENTS and what remains means put off; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To discourage or dissuade is to put someone off.

clue.text: In a race he is an ungodly type

indicators.note: In places the following words inside the race

parts.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
taken as written

explanation.surface: A competitor in a race is irreligious.
explanation.walkthrough: The TT (Tourist Trophy) is the motorbike race on the Isle of Man, a British crown dependency; the surface's 'race' means a contest, not a people.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who denies God's existence is without belief in any deity.

clue.text: String mislaid by Sir Arthur

parts.note: Sir Arthur Sullivan wrote a famous Victorian song about a musical sound found once and then never recovered

explanation.surface: A knighted gentleman has misplaced a piece of twine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'String' suggests cord or twine, but it is a musical combination of notes; Sir Arthur Sullivan's song is about one heard once and never found again.
explanation.definitionFit: Sullivan's well-known parlour song is titled after a musical harmony that the organist cannot find again.

clue.text: Room for a thrust? Nothing in it

indicators.note: in it says the nought goes inside the thrust

parts.note: a lunge is a thrust, as in fencing
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A fencer wonders if there is space to strike, and finds none.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A sitting room in a house is a living space.

clue.text: About 100 foolish fellows in the British Isles

indicators.note: About means the following word wraps around the number

parts.note: sillies are foolish people
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Around a hundred idiots live somewhere in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scilly Isles are an archipelago off Cornwall, the south-west tip of England.
explanation.definitionFit: The island group off Land's End lies within that archipelago.

clue.text: Laconic form of weather signals

indicators.note: form means the letters are given a new shape

explanation.surface: Weather warnings are given tersely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' rearranges LACONIC; storm warnings at British harbours were shown by hoisting cone shapes, hence the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Storm cones hoisted at coastguard stations had a tapering, cone-shaped outline.

clue.text: Might be fired if I ignored this regulation

indicators.note: if, with 'ignored' after the letter, says the answer is the artillery word once its I is put back in

parts.note: ordnance, artillery, is what gets fired

explanation.surface: A rule says someone might be dismissed for disregarding it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: ignore the I in the answer and ORDNANCE remains, so 'if' ... 'ignored' means ORDNANCE with I put in. 'fired' suggests dismissal, but it is guns going off.
explanation.definitionFit: A decree or bylaw issued by an authority is a rule.

clue.text: Make deep research as Adam was wont to do

definitions.text: as Adam was wont to do

explanation.surface: Adam is cast as a diligent researcher.
explanation.walkthrough: The old rhyme 'When Adam delved and Eve span' shows Adam digging the soil.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig is both to investigate thoroughly and, literally, to turn the earth as the first man did.

clue.text: Perfume distilled to touch a lip

indicators.note: distilling breaks a substance down and recombines it, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A scent is refined so that it can be dabbed on the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distilled' fits the perfume picture but is the anagram signal: TOUCHALIP rearranged; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An oily fragrance from an Asian mint plant, popular in scents and incense.

clue.text: Not like sound from synod altercation

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of the run of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A row at a church council is said to be anything but harmonious.
explanation.walkthrough: Look across the break in 'syNOD ALtercation'. 'Not like' also plays on 'knot-like', a node being a knot.
explanation.definitionFit: A node in a vibrating string is a still point that produces no vibration, so relating to such points means silence.

clue.text: Banned union does not need this

definitions.text: Banned union does not need this

parts.words: Banned union does not need this
parts.note: read 'Banned' as 'banns-ed': a wedding announced by banns read in church needs no separate legal permit

explanation.surface: A prohibited trade union has no use for some document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banned' looks like prohibited, but it means announced by banns in church, which makes a separate permit unnecessary.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple may marry after banns are called or with an official permit instead, so a banns wedding needs no such paper.

clue.text: Delicacy one caught in Tyne perhaps

indicators.note: the pair of letters goes inside the rearranged river name
perhaps signals that the river name is only one possible arrangement of its letters

parts.note: one is I as a Roman numeral
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A gourmet treat was landed in a north-east English river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' makes NETY from TYNE (a river in north-east England), and 'in' puts IC inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A delicacy is a fine distinction or subtle point, as is a nicety.

clue.text: One cautious in play?

parts.note: split as one who takes care, and recall Pinter's drama about a tramp taken in

explanation.surface: Someone careful in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Pinter's play is named for a building custodian; split the word and it means one who takes care.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinter's drama is named after a janitor, literally someone who exercises care.

clue.text: Girl in this Latin embrace is all Greek

indicators.note: the Latin word holds the girl's name within its arms

parts.note: hic is Latin for this
Ellen is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl wrapped in a Latin hug finds it all incomprehensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all Greek' plays on the idiom for not understanding, but here simply means Greek; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes things belonging to the people and culture of Hellas.

clue.text: First class state

parts.note: taken as written
first is one, I as a Roman numeral
Cal is an abbreviation of California, a US state

explanation.surface: A country in top condition.
explanation.walkthrough: CLASS I is first class, and CAL is California; together they mean of the highest rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Classical art is of the highest rank and lasting standard.

clue.text: Rebound, from a glance?

explanation.surface: Someone bounces back after a look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'glance' is not a look but a glancing blow, as when a bullet skims off a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A projectile skipping off a hard surface springs back, the result of a glancing strike.

clue.text: A conundrum, result of selecting the initial characters

definitions.text: result of selecting the initial characters

explanation.surface: A puzzle comes from picking the opening letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A word puzzle in verse where the first letters of the lines spell a hidden word, which is how such a composition is made.

clue.text: How would Thorndike's doctor deal with a fainting fit?

parts.note: Dr Syn is the smuggling vicar in Russell Thorndike's novels
to cope is to deal with

explanation.surface: A novelist's physician handles a patient who has collapsed.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Syn is the parson-smuggler hero of Russell Thorndike's novels; 'How would' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Syncope is the medical term for a brief loss of consciousness.

clue.text: Has a steep exchange rate

indicators.note: exchange means the letters trade places with one another

explanation.surface: A currency is said to have a punishing conversion rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchange rate' reads as one phrase, but 'exchange' turns ASTEEP into the old Spanish currency, and 'rate' is a loose definition; 'Has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The former unit of Spanish money was a currency with its own value against others.

clue.text: Get utmost out of broken meter

parts.note: ex is Latin for out of

indicators.note: broken means the letters are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: Getting a maximum reading from a damaged gauge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges METER to TREME; 'Get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The furthest or greatest degree is the ultimate limit.

clue.text: This cash return would do for a junket

indicators.note: return means the substance's name is read backwards

parts.note: rennet is used to curdle milk for the dessert junket

explanation.surface: Money given back would pay for a jaunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'junket' suggests a jolly trip but is a milk pudding set with rennet; 'return' makes it read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A ten-pound note is a sum of money.

clue.text: Wordy diet for one hoping to go to law

definitions.text: Wordy diet for one hoping to go to law

parts.words: Wordy diet for one hoping to go to law
parts.note: a trainee barrister must dine at an Inn of Court a set number of times; 'wordy' plays on terms as words

explanation.surface: A would-be lawyer is put on a diet of words.
explanation.walkthrough: Trainee barristers in England were required to eat a number of dinners at their Inn of Court each legal term; 'Wordy' puns on terms as words.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the idiom for a student barrister completing required dinners at an Inn of Court.

clue.text: Emma's suitor gave change for a pound note

indicators.note: giving change rearranges the letters into a new order

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pound, from libra

explanation.surface: A lover handed over coins for a banknote.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Elton is the vicar who courts Emma in Jane Austen's novel; 'gave change for' rearranges L and NOTE.
explanation.definitionFit: In Austen's novel the vicar proposes to the heroine, so he is her admirer.

clue.text: It spins and lifts both ways

indicators.note: both ways says the word reads the same backwards and forwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Something that whirls and raises reads identically either direction.
explanation.definitionFit: The rotating blades of a helicopter both turn and provide lift.

clue.text: Capital for which toy-maker receives approval

indicators.note: the maker here builds a new word out of the letters of toy and the approving word

parts.note: OK is a common way of giving approval

explanation.surface: A city where a manufacturer of playthings gets the nod.
explanation.walkthrough: 'toy-maker' looks like a manufacturer, but 'maker' rearranges TOY plus OK (the approval it 'receives'); 'for which' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese seat of government is a capital city.

clue.text: These towns were in league with the Germans

definitions.text: These towns were in league with the Germans

parts.words: These towns were in league with the Germans
parts.note: medieval trading towns of northern Germany and the Baltic formed a commercial league

explanation.surface: Some towns are accused of colluding with Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in league with' sounds like collusion, but refers literally to the medieval trading league of north German cities.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hanse was a medieval commercial federation of German and Baltic merchant towns.

clue.text: Almost the wind of Hamlet's madness

definitions.text: Almost the wind of Hamlet's madness

parts.words: Almost the wind of Hamlet's madness
parts.note: Hamlet says he is mad only north-north-west; drop one 'north' and you have the wind direction

explanation.surface: A breeze nearly matches the Danish prince's insanity.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says 'I am but mad north-north-west'; 'Almost' trims that to a single compass point, a gale from that quarter.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm blowing from the north-west quarter is named after its direction.

clue.text: Loner forced to become member

indicators.note: forced suggests the letters are pushed into a new order

explanation.surface: A solitary person is pressured into joining a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forced' rearranges LONER; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To sign up is to register as one of a group.
